catalog_quote: 1.4. Acento. En general el acento no se ha escrito en las palabras de este diccionario, ya que el popoluca tiene una regla de acentuación, la cual dice que las palabras terminadas en vocal llevan el acento prosódico en la penúltima sílaba y las palabras terminadas en consonante, en vocal con saltillo o en vocal con jota, llevan el acento prosódico en la última sílaba. Ejemplos: šʉvʉ [šʉ́vʉ] sol; šʉvʉ' [šʉvʉ́'] está viejo; aucʉ'm [aucʉ́'m] en frente de; na'cšicoj [na'cšicój] antes. [p. 111:] Cuando la letra u le sigue a otra vocal se considera como consonante. Es por eso que el acento recae en la última sílaba en los siguientes ejemplos: majau [majáu] mujer; jayma'jiu [jayma'jíu] difunto. Las palabras que no siguen esta regla llevan acento escrito. Por ejemplo: ime̱ñuwocʉ̱́ 'sus centavitos'. En el tiempo futuro el acento prosódico recae en el sufijo. En este caso se usa el acento escrito. En los otros tiempos del verbo el acento recae en la raíz misma y no se escribe. Ejemplos: tʉmapa estoy durmiendo; tʉmaju dormí; tʉma'jám voy a dormir.

new_statements.translation: 1.4. Stress. In general stress has not been written on the words of this dictionary, since Popoluca has a stress rule, which says that words ending in a vowel carry the prosodic stress on the penultimate syllable, and words ending in a consonant, in a vowel with glottal stop (saltillo) or in a vowel with j [h], carry the prosodic stress on the last syllable. Examples: šʉvʉ [šʉ́vʉ] 'sun'; šʉvʉ' [šʉvʉ́'] 'is old'; aucu'm [aucú'm] 'in front of'; na'cšicoj [na'cšicój] 'before'. [p.111:] When the letter u follows another vowel it is considered a consonant. That is why stress falls on the last syllable in the following examples: majau [majáu] 'woman' ... Words that do not follow this rule carry a written accent, e.g. ime̱nuwocʉ́ 'his little cents'. In the future tense the prosodic stress falls on the suffix.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Right-edge, closure-sensitive: stress the final syllable if the word ends in a consonant (including postvocalic w/u), in Vʔ or in Vh; otherwise (word ends in a plain short or long vowel) stress the penult. Equivalent to 'final if the last syllable is closed, else penultimate'.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical exceptions exist and are marked with a written acute in the dictionary (e.g. ime̱nuwocʉ́ 'sus centavitos', final stress on an open syllable). Future suffix -am always bears stress (written tʉma'jám; consistent with the C-final rule), other tenses have stress on the root. §1.6.3.6 (p.115): the narrative enclitic -c/-ac 'no causa ningún cambio en el acento, a pesar de que termina en consonante' — explicitly called the exception to the stress rule (tu'coc tʉn-iti [tú'coc tʉn-íti]).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated for dictionary citation forms and inflected verbs; used as the basis for an orthographic convention (accent written only on exceptions and on the future suffix). No discussion of phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Clark 1981 describes 'popoluca de Oluta' = Oluteco/Olutec, the single-town language of Oluta, Veracruz (olut1240, ISO plo); same variety as Zavala's 'Oluteco'. No dialect split involved. Clark's orthography: ʉ = high central/back unrounded vowel, underlining = length, ' = glottal stop, j = [h], postvocalic u = /w/.

sources.note: §1.4: explicit rule — words ending in a vowel are stressed on the penult; words ending in a consonant, in V+glottal stop (saltillo) or V+j [h] are stressed on the final syllable; postvocalic u counts as a consonant (majáu); exceptions carry a written accent (ime̱nuwocʉ́); future suffix takes the stress (tʉma'jám); §1.6.3.6: narrative enclitic -c/-ac does not shift stress (stated exception).
